conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Patel, one of the hospitalists. You were brought in last night with abdominal pain and trouble breathing. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, doc. I started feeling this pain in my upper belly a few days ago. It goes to my back, and I’ve been nauseous, throwing up nothing—just dry heaves. And I’ve been wheezing a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I felt feverish. And I did start drinking again a few days ago. I know it’s not smart, but I was stressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for being honest. We also noticed you hadn’t gotten your methadone recently because of the breathing issues?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. I couldn’t get to the clinic. I’ve been on 80 mg daily at Habit OPCO.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve restarted your methadone. We’re also watching you for alcohol withdrawal. You had some tremors, but you’re not in severe withdrawal right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had bad withdrawals before—seizures once. I don’t want that again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring you closely with a scale called CIWA. You got a small dose of Ativan earlier, and we’ll taper that as needed. You’re safe here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. What about the belly pain? Feels worse than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan of your abdomen. It didn’t show pancreatitis or any serious issue. Your lipase was only slightly high. We think this is likely alcoholic gastritis—irritation from drinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not my pancreas again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the pancreas looks normal on the scan. We’re treating it as stomach inflammation for now. You were on IV fluids and Dilaudid overnight. Now that you’re tolerating sips, we’ll switch to oral pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The IV pain med didn’t help much. Can I get something stronger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We have to be careful. You’re on methadone and Ativan, which can make you drowsy. We don’t want to risk breathing problems. We’ll keep adjusting, but safety comes first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I get it, but the pain’s real.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I believe you. We’ll keep monitoring and make sure you’re as comfortable as possible. Now, about your breathing—you were wheezing a lot in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had asthma since I was a kid. I’ve even been intubated before. Scary stuff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you albuterol treatments—Duonebs—and a steroid, prednisone, to reduce inflammation. Your breathing is better today, and your chest X-ray showed no pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I was worried it was an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of infection. We’re giving you azithromycin just in case, and continuing your inhalers. We think the asthma flare might be from aspiration—maybe when you were drinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could be. I did cough a lot after drinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fits. We’ll keep treating the asthma until you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. I’m checking in. How’s the pain and breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Breathing’s better. Pain’s still there, but I guess it’s not as bad as last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your labs came back. Liver enzymes are elevated—AST is high, and alkaline phosphatase is in the 900s. But that’s been high before, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, my liver’s been messed up for years. Cirrhosis, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the CT confirms cirrhosis, with varices and an enlarged spleen. But no new tumors or blockages. Your liver is stable, not in acute failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing new?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No acute issues. The high alkaline phosphatase is chronic. We’re not concerned about a bile duct blockage since your MRCP last time was clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my stomach? I keep having these pain episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s chronic gastritis from alcohol and possibly CMV, based on past biopsies. After you’re discharged, you should get an EGD to check your stomach and varices.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had those before. Not fun, but I’ll do it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll refer you. Depending on what they find, you might need a beta-blocker like nadolol to prevent variceal bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You’re doing well. We’re stopping the Ativan—you’re no longer in withdrawal. CIWA score has been zero for 12 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel more clear-headed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver enzymes are starting to trend down. AST is lower today. We’ll keep you on your usual liver meds—furosemide and spironolactone—but restart them at home since you weren’t eating much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I forgot to take my thiamine and folic acid the last few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving those here. You need them, especially with your history. We’ll make sure you have them filled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re almost ready to go home. Your breathing is normal, pain is manageable, and you’re off withdrawal meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before: methadone 80 mg daily, acamprosate, your inhalers, pantoprazole for stomach protection. Plus a one-day prednisone burst and azithromycin for the asthma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get two days of hydrocodone—2 mg every six hours as needed. But please use it sparingly. We want to avoid dependency issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I just don’t want to end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Staying off alcohol is the best way to avoid that. It’s causing your gastritis, liver issues, and even the asthma flare. We can help you connect with a recovery program.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve tried before. It’s hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get you support. Your counselor will call you this week. And please follow up with your liver doctor and get that EGD scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today. You’ve improved a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I feel way better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: take your meds, avoid alcohol, use your inhalers, and call your doctor if breathing or pain gets worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll call about the EGD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and we’re here if you need us.
